> **Key takeaways**
> - Send one short welcome message after booking. Cover what to bring, parking, who meets them, how long class runs and the first ten minutes.
> - Ask the parent what helps their child settle, and take the answer at face value.
> - Plan the arrival for a first-timer, offer a buddy or a watch-first option, and send a two-line note after class.

## Why the days before the first class matter

A family that has just booked is excited and a little unsure. Most of their worries, from parking to who the teacher is, can be answered before they arrive, with a welcome that is short, clear and sent at the right time.

## Send a short welcome message after booking

Send it soon after the booking comes in, while the class is fresh in the parent's mind. Cover only what a parent needs to get there and settle in:

- **What to bring.** Clothes, shoes, a water bottle, anything your activity needs. Say what they don't need, too.
- **Where to park,** and which entrance to use.
- **Who meets them.** A first name and a role: "Ana, our lead teacher, will meet you at the front desk."
- **How long it runs,** and when to arrive. A few minutes early is usually right for a first visit.
- **What the first ten minutes look like.** This settles a nervous child more than anything else. "We start with a name game, then a short warm-up" gives a parent something to tell their child on the drive over.
- **Whether parents stay or drop off.**

Here is a template to adapt. Swap the parts in brackets for your own details.

> **Template: welcome message after booking**
>
> Hi [parent's name], thanks for booking [child's name] into [class name] on [day] at [time]. We're looking forward to meeting you both.
>
> - **Bring:** [clothes, shoes, water bottle].
> - **Parking:** [where to park and which entrance to use].
> - **Who meets you:** [name], our [role], at [spot].
> - **How long:** [length]. Please arrive about [a few] minutes early the first time.
> - **The first ten minutes:** [for example, a name game and a short warm-up].
> - **Parents:** [you're welcome to stay / drop-off is fine].
>
> Is there anything that helps [child's name] settle into something new? Just reply here.

## Ask what helps the child

That last line matters most. A parent knows what helps their child settle: arriving before the room fills up, knowing where the bathroom is, holding a familiar object, or a minute to watch first.

Ask openly and take the answer at face value. Don't guess at reasons, and don't ask for medical details. If a parent has set a support preference on the booking, such as a sensory-friendly setting, treat it as a reason to ask what works for that child, not as a label that tells you what to expect. Two children with the same preference may need quite different things. Share what the parent tells you only with staff who need it to run the class.

## Plan the arrival for a first-timer

Regular families know the routine. A first-timer doesn't, so make arrival easy to follow:

- **Make the entrance easy to find.** A small sign, or one clear detail in your message ("the blue door next to the cafe"), saves a lost family ten minutes.
- **Greet the child by name,** and show them where shoes and bags go.
- **Keep check-in short.** Paperwork should be done before the day, or take a minute at most.
- **Explain pick-up** before the parent leaves, and release each child only to the adult who dropped them off or one the parent named.

## Offer a buddy or a watch-first option

Some children need a moment. Two simple options help without singling anyone out:

- **A buddy.** Pair the new child with a friendly regular of a similar age for the warm-up. Ask the regular quietly beforehand; most children like being asked to help.
- **Watch first.** Let the child sit and watch for a few minutes, close enough to join when ready, and tell them that's fine. Many children join on their own once they see what the activity looks like.

Mention both in your welcome message, so the parent knows these are normal options and not a sign that something has gone wrong.

## Send a quick note after the first class

A short note the same day closes the loop. Give one specific thing the child did and one thing that happens next time. "She led the warm-up line" means more than "she did great".

> **Template: note after the first class**
>
> Hi [parent's name], thanks for bringing [child's name] today. [One specific thing, for example: "He tried the cartwheel drill three times and got further each go."] Next week we'll [what comes next]. See you then.

If the first class was hard, say so kindly and plainly, and suggest one small thing for next time, such as arriving a little earlier. Our post on [how to get more students for your kids' classes](/blog/how-to-get-more-students-for-kids-classes) covers more ways to keep new families coming back.

## Keep messages short and adult to adult

Your messages go to the parent, not the child. Write the way you would talk at the front desk:

- **Short beats complete.** Four lines a parent can read in a parking lot beat a page they skim.
- **One message, one purpose.** Don't fold a sales pitch into a welcome.
- **Plain words.** Skip your activity's jargon until the family has learned it.

Put the same practical details in your listing, so families see them before they book. Our guide to [writing a kids' class listing parents actually book](/blog/how-to-write-a-kids-class-listing-parents-book) shows what to include.

## FAQ

### When should I send a welcome message to a new family?

Soon after the booking comes in. That gives the family time to ask questions and get ready before the day.

### What should a first class welcome message for parents include?

What to bring, where to park, who meets them, how long class runs, when to arrive, what the first ten minutes look like, and whether parents stay. End by asking what helps their child settle.

### How do I ask about a child's needs without prying?

Ask one open question: "Is there anything that helps your child settle into something new?" Take the answer at face value, don't ask for medical details, and share it only with staff who need it.

### What if a child won't join in at the first class?

Offer a watch-first spot close to the group, or a friendly regular as a buddy. Tell the child they can join when ready, and let the parent know this is normal.
